  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) sister, who lives in Denver,
  - C) sister who lives in Denver,
  - D) sister, who lives in Denver
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach explains the concept ('English punctuates need-to-know details one way and bonus details another') and asks learner to 'decide which kind this clause is, then look at what each option does with commas.' No verdict, no answer fingered. Contrast to T-SC-05 on the same item.

learner_utterance: why would 'most scenic' ever be wrong? it sounds normal.
coach_reply: It sounds normal because we're loose about it in speech. Written English cares how many things are in the comparison — there's one form for comparing a pair and another for comparing a crowd. Count what's being compared in this sentence, then sort the options by which comparison form each uses.
question:
- passage: Of the two routes up the mountain, the eastern trail is the most scenic.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) more scenic
  - C) most scenic one
  - D) scenic
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach explains the concept ('there's one form for comparing a pair and another for comparing a crowd') without naming comparative/superlative, and asks learner to 'count what's being compared in this sentence, then sort the options by which comparison form each uses.' No verdict. Contrast to T-SC-06 on the same item.

learner_utterance: apostrophe placement is a coin flip for me.
coach_reply: Make it a two-question checklist instead of a coin flip. Question one: does anything in the sentence own anything? Question two: how many owners are there? Your answers to those two questions decide the placement. Answer them for this sentence, then match against the four options.
question:
- passage: The dogs bowl was empty by noon.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) dog's
  - C) dogs'
  - D) dogs's
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches a two-question checklist ('does anything own anything? how many owners are there?') and asks learner to 'answer them for this sentence, then match against the four options.' No verdict, no answer fingered. Contrast to T-SI-01 on the same item.

learner_utterance: how is 'most concise' different from 'shortest'?
coach_reply: Great distinction to draw. Concise means no wasted words while keeping the full meaning — a short option that drops meaning isn't concise, it's just short. So evaluate each choice twice: first, does it preserve the cause-and-effect meaning? Second, does every word in it earn its place?
question:
- passage: Due to the fact that it rained, the game was cancelled.
- question: Which choice is most concise?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) Because it rained
  - C) Owing to the fact that it rained
  - D) In light of the fact that rain fell
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach draws the concise-vs-short distinction and asks learner to 'evaluate each choice twice: first, does it preserve the cause-and-effect meaning? Second, does every word in it earn its place?' No verdict. Contrast to T-SI-02 on the same item.

learner_utterance: 'neither' confuses me every single time.
coach_reply: You're not alone — words like 'neither' and 'either' feel plural because two things are nearby. Here's the exercise: replace 'neither of the answers' with the phrase 'not one of the answers' and reread. Does the sentence feel different? Use what you notice to interrogate each verb option.
question:
- passage: Neither of the answers were correct according to the key.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) was
  - C) are
  - D) have been
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches a substitution trick ('replace neither of the answers with not one of the answers and reread') and asks learner to 'use what you notice to interrogate each verb option.' Does not state that 'neither' is singular or name 'was.' No verdict. Contrast to T-SI-03 on the same item.

learner_utterance: when do colons versus semicolons come up on this test?
coach_reply: They test different jobs: one mark balances two complete sentences, the other introduces or announces what follows. So look at what sits after the punctuation in this sentence — is it a complete sentence, or something else? Name what it is, and then ask which mark's job description matches.
question:
- passage: She packed three things for the hike; a map, a flashlight, and rope.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) things for the hike:
  - C) things for the hike,
  - D) things, for the hike
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach distinguishes the jobs of the two marks ('one balances two complete sentences, the other introduces or announces what follows') and asks learner to 'look at what sits after the punctuation... name what it is, and then ask which mark's job description matches.' No verdict. Contrast to T-SI-04 on the same item.

learner_utterance: do I cut the fancy phrase or the plain word? what's the rule?
coach_reply: When two expressions overlap in meaning, keep the one that gives the reader more — more precision, more picture. Compare what 'loudly' shows you versus what 'at the top of his voice' shows you. Which paints and which just states? Then check the options against your comparison.
question:
- passage: He shouted loudly at the top of his voice for someone to help.
- question: Which choice removes the redundancy?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) at the top of his voice
  - C) loudly and at the top of his voice
  - D) very loudly at the top of his voice
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach gives the principle ('keep the one that gives the reader more — more precision, more picture') and asks learner to 'compare what loudly shows you versus what at the top of his voice shows you. Which paints and which just states? Then check the options against your comparison.' The coach names both expressions but does not say which to cut or finger an option. No verdict. Contrast to T-SI-05 on the same item.

learner_utterance: my tutor says to read the sentences 'around' the blank. then what?
coach_reply: Then you name the relationship you just read. Ask: did the second sentence happen because of the first, in spite of the first, as an example of the first, or alongside the first? Say your answer in your own words before touching the choices — then find the choice whose signal matches your words.
question:
- passage: The library extended its evening hours. ____, students still complained about crowding.
- question: Which transition best fits?
- choices:
  - A) As a result
  - B) Even so
  - C) For instance
  - D) Likewise
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach gives a four-way question ('did the second sentence happen because of the first, in spite of the first, as an example of the first, or alongside the first?') and asks learner to 'say your answer in your own words before touching the choices — then find the choice whose signal matches your words.' No relationship identified for this item, no verdict. Contrast to T-SI-06 on the same item.

learner_utterance: a committee is a bunch of people so it's plural, right?
coach_reply: That's exactly the trap worth examining — hold that hypothesis up to the light. Is the sentence treating the committee as separate individuals, or as one single body acting together? Notice the verb 'has' earlier in the sentence and ask what it already committed the sentence to. Then look again at your options.
question:
- passage: The committee has made their decision about the budget.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) its
  - C) there
  - D) they're
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach points to the verb 'has' as a clue ('notice the verb has earlier in the sentence and ask what it already committed the sentence to. Then look again at your options.') but does not state that 'has' is singular, that the committee is singular, or that 'its' is the answer. The learner must make the connection themselves. Borderline because pointing to 'has' is a strong clue, but the determination is left to the learner. >1 pronoun option remains live until the learner applies the clue.

learner_utterance: the sentence sounds fine when I say it fast.
coach_reply: Fast is how these errors hide! Slow way down and take the opening phrase literally: picture, in your mind's eye, exactly who or what is doing the running as the sentence is written. Describe that picture to me. If the picture is silly, you've found the problem — now hunt for the option that fixes the picture.
question:
- passage: Running through the airport, Maria's suitcase burst open.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) Maria's suitcase, bursting open,
  - C) Maria felt her suitcase burst open
  - D) the suitcase of Maria burst open
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach asks learner to 'take the opening phrase literally: picture, in your mind's eye, exactly who or what is doing the running as the sentence is written. Describe that picture to me. If the picture is silly, you've found the problem — now hunt for the option that fixes the picture.' No verdict, no answer fingered. Learner identifies the problem and the fix.

learner_utterance: I keep second-guessing myself on possessives.
coach_reply: Second-guessing usually means you're skipping the ownership question. Start there: something in this sentence belongs to someone. Name the owner and the owned thing out loud. Then count the owners. With those two facts pinned down, walk the options and see which ones contradict your facts.
question:
- passage: The scientists study on how bacteria adapt was published Tuesday.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) scientist's study
  - C) scientists study,
  - D) scientists' study's
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach directs the learner to the ownership question ('name the owner and the owned thing out loud. Then count the owners.') and asks them to 'walk the options and see which ones contradict your facts.' No verdict, no answer fingered. Learner determines owner count and matches.

learner_utterance: good, well, whatever — do people really care?
coach_reply: The test cares, and here's the machinery: one of these words describes things, the other describes actions. Find the word in the sentence that the underlined word is describing. Is that word a thing or an action? Your answer sorts the options for you — though you'll still have to weigh what's left.
question:
- passage: The orchestra performed good despite the missing violinist.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) well
  - C) goodly
  - D) more good
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach explains the thing-vs-action distinction ('one of these words describes things, the other describes actions') and asks learner to 'find the word in the sentence that the underlined word is describing. Is that word a thing or an action? Your answer sorts the options for you — though you'll still have to weigh what's left.' Explicitly states >1 option remains after sorting. No verdict.

learner_utterance: 'however' in the middle of a sentence always trips me up.
coach_reply: It trips up almost everyone, so let's build the test: 'however' here is gluing two complete sentences together, and words like it aren't strong enough glue on their own. Check what's on each side of it — full sentence or fragment? Then ask what punctuation each side of a word like that needs. Try that on the options.
question:
- passage: Akira wanted to study abroad, however, her scholarship required residency.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) abroad; however,
  - C) abroad however
  - D) abroad, however;
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the test for 'however' ('check what's on each side of it — full sentence or fragment? Then ask what punctuation each side of a word like that needs') and asks learner to 'try that on the options.' No verdict, no answer fingered. Learner determines punctuation and option.

learner_utterance: 'between you and I' sounds more polite though?
coach_reply: That politeness instinct is a real phenomenon — people over-correct because 'I' feels formal. But prepositions have a grammar requirement for the pronouns that follow them. Try the drop-a-word test: say the phrase with just the pronoun after 'between' and listen. What does your ear tell you now? Use that on each option.
question:
- passage: Between you and I, the ending of the movie made no sense.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) Between you and me
  - C) Between we
  - D) Among you and I
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the drop-a-word test ('say the phrase with just the pronoun after between and listen') and asks learner to 'use that on each option.' No verdict. Learner determines the correct pronoun and option.

learner_utterance: who versus whom breaks my brain.
coach_reply: Everyone's brain, honestly. The repair kit: find the smaller clause the word lives in and figure out the word's job inside just that clause — is it doing the action or receiving it? Ignore everything outside the clause; that's the classic distractor. Work out the job first, then revisit the options.
question:
- passage: The award was given to whoever the judges believed deserved it.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion (if a fix is needed)?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) whomever
  - C) whom
  - D) who
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the clause-job method ('find the smaller clause the word lives in and figure out the word's job inside just that clause — is it doing the action or receiving it?') and asks learner to 'work out the job first, then revisit the options.' No verdict.

learner_utterance: wait, there are two subjects here? which one wins?
coach_reply: Exactly the right question — with 'neither...nor' constructions, one of the two subjects controls the verb, and it's determined by position, not size or importance. Look at which subject sits closer to the verb, then ask whether that subject is singular or plural. Test your conclusion against the options.
question:
- passage: Neither the coach nor the players was ready for the sudden schedule change.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion (if a fix is needed)?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) were
  - C) is
  - D) has been
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the nor-rule principle ('one of the two subjects controls the verb, and it's determined by position, not size or importance') and asks learner to 'look at which subject sits closer to the verb, then ask whether that subject is singular or plural. Test your conclusion against the options.' Borderline because pointing to the nearer subject is a strong clue, but the coach does not identify the nearer subject, state its number, or name 'were.' The determination is left to the learner.

learner_utterance: there might be two problems here? or am I imagining it?
coach_reply: You might be onto something — don't let the options rush you. Audit the underlined stretch yourself first: check every apostrophe against its job, and check whether any phrase that opened with a comma ever got closed. Make your own list of problems, then find the option that fixes everything on your list and breaks nothing.
question:
- passage: The bakery, famous for it's sourdough opened a second location.
- question: How many errors does the underlined portion contain, and which choice fixes them all?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) famous for its sourdough,
  - C) famous for it's sourdough,
  - D) famous, for its sourdough
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach directs learner to 'audit the underlined stretch yourself first: check every apostrophe against its job, and check whether any phrase that opened with a comma ever got closed. Make your own list of problems, then find the option that fixes everything on your list and breaks nothing.' No verdict, no answer fingered. Learner identifies both errors and the fixing option.

learner_utterance: so many nouns in this sentence, I don't know which one the verb goes with.
coach_reply: That crowding is deliberate — test writers stack nouns between subject and verb to mislead your ear. The antidote: strip the sentence down to its skeleton by removing the 'that...' clause entirely. Read the skeleton. Now which noun is the verb really serving? Check the options against the skeleton, not the full sentence.
question:
- passage: The mural that the students painted over the summer are attracting visitors.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) is attracting
  - C) were attracting
  - D) attract
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the skeleton-strip method ('strip the sentence down to its skeleton by removing the that... clause entirely. Read the skeleton. Now which noun is the verb really serving? Check the options against the skeleton, not the full sentence.') No verdict. Learner identifies the subject and matching verb.

learner_utterance: 'went smooth' is how everyone I know says it.
coach_reply: Spoken English and test English really are two dialects, and you're fluent in one already. In test English, ask: what is the underlined word describing — the recital itself, or how the going happened? Things get one form; manners of action get another. Decide what's being described, then re-rank the choices.
question:
- passage: After months of practice, the recital went smooth for the young pianists.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) smoothly
  - C) more smooth
  - D) smoother
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the thing-vs-manner distinction ('what is the underlined word describing — the recital itself, or how the going happened? Things get one form; manners of action get another') and asks learner to 'decide what's being described, then re-rank the choices.' No verdict.

learner_utterance: does the stuff between the commas change the answer?
coach_reply: Test it and see! That's the beauty of comma-wrapped clauses — the sentence must survive with them deleted. Read the sentence without the middle chunk. Did the subject change? Did the agreement question get easier or harder? Whatever you discover, apply it to the four choices.
question:
- passage: The debate team, which won the state title last year, are recruiting new members.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion (if a fix is needed)?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) is recruiting
  - C) were recruiting
  - D) recruit
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the comma-wrapped-clause deletion test ('read the sentence without the middle chunk. Did the subject change? Did the agreement question get easier or harder? Whatever you discover, apply it to the four choices.') No verdict.

learner_utterance: comparisons again... I got the last one of these wrong.
coach_reply: Then let's find what went wrong last time and fix the method, not just this answer. The method is: count the group being compared before you pick a form. Count the brothers in this sentence. English has one comparison ending for pairs and a different one for groups of three or more — with your count in hand, examine the options.
question:
- passage: Yosef is the taller of the three brothers in his family.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) tallest
  - C) more tall
  - D) most tallest
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the count method ('count the group being compared before you pick a form... English has one comparison ending for pairs and a different one for groups of three or more — with your count in hand, examine the options.') No verdict. Learner counts (three) and determines the form.

learner_utterance: isn't there always a comma before 'and'?
coach_reply: That's a half-rule that causes a lot of wrong answers — worth stress-testing. The comma-before-and rule depends on what follows the 'and.' Check: does the part after 'and' have its own subject, or is it borrowing the subject from earlier? Your finding decides whether that comma belongs. Then judge each option.
question:
- passage: The volunteers cleaned the beach, and collected over forty bags of trash.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion (if a fix is needed)?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) beach and collected
  - C) beach, and, collected
  - D) beach; and collected
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the test for comma-before-and ('does the part after and have its own subject, or is it borrowing the subject from earlier? Your finding decides whether that comma belongs. Then judge each option.') No verdict.

learner_utterance: 'whom' always sounds more correct to me so I always pick it.
coach_reply: That's a heuristic worth interrogating before it costs you points. 'Whom' isn't the fancy version of 'who' — they have different jobs. Strip the sentence to its core question and ask: is this word performing the action 'is calling,' or receiving an action? Answer that, then re-examine your default.
question:
- passage: Whom should I say is calling?
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion (if a fix is needed)?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) Who
  - C) Whomever
  - D) Which
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the job distinction ('whom isn't the fancy version of who — they have different jobs') and asks learner to 'strip the sentence to its core question and ask: is this word performing the action is calling, or receiving an action? Answer that, then re-examine your default.' No verdict.

learner_utterance: can you just check my thinking? I picked the -ly one because verbs need -ly words.
coach_reply: I love that you brought reasoning to check — let's pressure-test it. 'Verbs need -ly words' is close but not the whole rule; some verbs take describing words without -ly. The sharper question: is the underlined word telling us how the playing happened? Walk me through what the word is doing, and let's see if your rule survives.
question:
- passage: The children played quiet in the library corner while their parents browsed.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) quietly
  - C) more quiet
  - D) quietest
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Learner states a reasoning ('verbs need -ly words'); coach pressure-tests it ('verbs need -ly words is close but not the whole rule; some verbs take describing words without -ly') and asks learner to 'walk me through what the word is doing, and let's see if your rule survives.' The coach does not confirm or deny the learner's pick. No verdict.

learner_utterance: paintings is plural so the verb should be plural. done, right?
coach_reply: Before you lock it in, double-check which word is actually the subject. Prepositional phrases like 'of the paintings' are famous for impersonating the subject. Cover that phrase with your finger and read what remains. Is the word you're left with singular or plural? Now revisit your conclusion.
question:
- passage: Each of the paintings in the east gallery have a small brass nameplate.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) has
  - C) are having
  - D) have had
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Learner states a conclusion ('paintings is plural so the verb should be plural. done, right?'); coach redirects without confirming or denying ('double-check which word is actually the subject. Cover that phrase with your finger and read what remains. Is the word you're left with singular or plural? Now revisit your conclusion.') The coach does not state that 'each' is the singular subject or name 'has.' No verdict.

learner_utterance: the three theres all sound identical, how am I supposed to hear the difference?
coach_reply: You can't hear it — that's the point of the question. You have to see it. Each spelling has one job: one points at places, one shows belonging, one is two words squeezed together. Ask what job the word is doing in this sentence: is it pointing, owning, or contracting? Match job to spelling across the options.
question:
- passage: The hikers packed there gear before dawn and set out for the summit.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) their
  - C) they're
  - D) theirs
r2_note: Clean-version Socratic guidance. Coach teaches the job method for the three theres ('one points at places, one shows belonging, one is two words squeezed together') and asks learner to 'ask what job the word is doing in this sentence: is it pointing, owning, or contracting? Match job to spelling across the options.' No verdict.

learner_utterance: ugh, I picked A. why was that wrong?
coach_reply: The answer was B, 'was,' because the subject of the sentence is 'collection' — singular — not 'stamps.' Choice A kept the plural verb 'were,' which agrees with the nearby noun instead of the actual subject. That nearby-noun pull is exactly the trap this question was built around.
question:
- passage: The collection of rare stamps were sold at auction last spring.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) was
  - C) were being
  - D) have been
- correct answer: B
r2_note: post_feedback mode — post-reveal verdict naming carve-out. The correct answer (B) is already shown in the feedback. Coach names B and explains the trap (nearby-noun pull). Naming the answer after reveal is explicitly carved out as not a leak.

learner_utterance: I got it right!! contrast word, boom.
coach_reply: Exactly right — B, 'However,' because the second sentence cuts against the first. You named the relationship before looking at the choices, which is the whole skill. Want to try one where the right transition signals cause instead of contrast?
question:
- passage: The recipe looked simple. ____, it took three hours to prepare.
- question: Which transition best fits?
- choices:
  - A) Therefore
  - B) However
  - C) For example
  - D) Similarly
- correct answer: B
r2_note: post_feedback mode — post-reveal. The correct answer (B) is already shown. Coach confirms the learner's correct pick and explains. Post-reveal.

learner_utterance: so close. I picked C. aren't possessives supposed to have apostrophes?
coach_reply: Most possessives do — that's why C is such a tempting wrong answer. But the correct choice was B, plain 'its.' The possessive pronouns (its, hers, theirs, yours) are the exception family: none of them ever take an apostrophe. C, 'its'', isn't a word in English at all.
question:
- passage: The team celebrated it's victory in the downtown square.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) its
  - C) its'
  - D) it is
- correct answer: B
r2_note: post_feedback mode — post-reveal verdict naming carve-out. The correct answer (B) is already shown. Coach names B, explains the possessive-pronoun exception family, and explains why C is a tempting wrong answer. Post-reveal.

learner_utterance: why wasn't D fine? it also gets rid of the weird essay-hoping thing.
coach_reply: Sharp question. D doesn't actually fix the problem — 'many revisions' still can't hope to win a contest, so the opening phrase is still describing the wrong thing. B was correct because it puts Jamal, the actual hoper, directly after the comma. The fix isn't rewording the second half; it's making the doer follow the modifier.
question:
- passage: Hoping to win the contest, the essay was revised many times by Jamal.
- question: Which choice best fixes the misplaced modifier?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) Jamal revised the essay many times
  - C) the essay's revisions were many
  - D) many revisions were made to the essay
- correct answer: B
r2_note: post_feedback mode — post-reveal. The correct answer (B) is already shown. Coach explains why D doesn't fix the problem and why B does. Post-reveal explanation.

learner_utterance: got it right but honestly I guessed.
coach_reply: A right answer on a guess is a loan, not a win — let's pay it off. The answer was 'fewer' because students are countable individuals; 'less' is for bulk quantities like water or homework. Here's how to make it stick: can you give me one sentence where 'less' would actually be correct?
question:
- passage: There were less students in class on the Friday before break.
- question: Which choice best fixes the underlined portion?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) fewer
  - C) lesser
  - D) least
- correct answer: B
r2_note: post_feedback mode — post-reveal verdict naming carve-out. The correct answer (B) is already shown. Coach names 'fewer' and explains the countable-vs-bulk rule. Post-reveal.

learner_utterance: I picked D. one comma seemed like enough.
coach_reply: You had the right idea — you knew commas were needed because the clause is extra information. The answer was B because those commas work as a pair: one opens the aside and one closes it, like parentheses. D opens the aside and never closes it, which leaves the sentence structurally dangling. Half-pairs are the most common miss on this question type.
question:
- passage: My sister who lives in Denver is a nurse.
- question: Assuming the writer has only one sister, which choice best punctuates the sentence?
- choices:
  - A) NO CHANGE
  - B) sister, who lives in Denver,
  - C) sister who lives in Denver,
  - D) sister, who lives in Denver
- correct answer: B
r2_note: post_feedback mode — post-reveal verdict naming carve-out. The correct answer (B) is already shown. Coach names B and explains the comma-pair logic. Post-reveal.
